cur:catacombs2-cyriaca-denial-of-peter.summary: Two figures in tunic and pallium face each other on a damaged wall, with a large cockerel between them: Christ and Peter at the moment when Christ foretells that before the cock crows Peter will deny him three times. Both raise a hand, one in speech and the other in protest or dismay. The scene, common on sarcophagi, is much rarer in catacomb painting.
facts: The handwritten label on this University of Louvain glass slide reads 'Rome Cyriaque. 350–400. Négation de S. Pierre. Wilpert 242'.
Peter with the cockerel became a standard Christian image in the 4th century, appearing on many Roman sarcophagi.
cur:catacombs2-cyriaca-denial-of-peter.notes: The Leuven catalogue gives the location only as 'Catacomba (?)'; the attribution to the Catacomb of Cyriaca rests on the slide's handwritten label. Which of the two figures is Christ cannot be determined with certainty from the reproduction.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-canticle-hannah.summary: A half-figure of the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos in a mandorla among six angels presides over the Song of Hannah. Below him the poor man is set on the 'throne of glory' among princes and crowned by the Hand of God, the barren woman appears with her seven children, and in a central circle Hannah stands among mighty kings whose bows lie broken. At the bottom an angel brings souls up from the pit while a demon pushes the wicked down: 'the Lord killeth, and maketh alive'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-canticle-hannah.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-valcavado-christ-angel-.summary: The opening picture of the Apocalypse cycle shows how the revelation passes from Christ to his angel and from the angel to John: Christ hands over the book, the angel carries it on, and John receives it below, as the first verse says, 'The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him ... and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John'. Bold bands of colour and great-eyed figures are typical of Oveco's painting.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
Beatus of Liébana compiled his Commentary on the Apocalypse in the late 8th century; its illustrated copies form one of the great cycles of early Spanish painting.
cur:manuscripts2-valcavado-christ-angel-.notes: Identification of the scene follows the file title and the standard Beatus iconography of Revelation 1:1; the painted surface is somewhat worn.

cur:objects-bologna-whalebone-christ-ent.summary: Christ sits on a high-backed throne with a bolster cushion, his feet on a footstool, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a book on his knee. Plant scrolls fill the background on either side of the throne. Carved not from elephant ivory but from whale bone, the plaque shows how the image of Christ in majesty was reproduced in more modest materials.
facts: Whale bone and walrus ivory were used as substitutes when elephant ivory was scarce, particularly in the West in the 10th and 11th centuries (type).
cur:objects-bologna-whalebone-christ-ent.notes: Place of production is uncertain; the museum caption gives only 'mid-10th century, whale bone'.

walters:42.1343.summary: A red carnelian set in a simple gold ring is engraved with the Good Shepherd: a standing youth carries a sheep across his shoulders while two more sheep stand at his feet, between small trees. According to the Walters the ring also bears an anchor with a Christian monogram on one side and a vine on the other, marking it clearly as a Christian's possession. Pressed into wax as a seal, the image proclaimed its owner's trust in Christ the shepherd.
facts: The ring was once owned by the archaeologist Sir Arthur Evans (his inventory no. 219) and was said to come from Catania in Sicily.
After Evans's death it passed through his executor Jacob Hirsch to Saidie A. May, who gave it to the Walters in 1942.
walters:42.1343.notes: The anchor and vine described by the museum are not visible in the frontal photograph. Date: 4th century (museum).

wga:zearly/2/2paintin/5oberze5.summary: Two linked miracles unfold in one long panel: at the left Christ turns to the woman who has touched the hem of his garment, and then, with his disciples and Jairus, moves toward the house at the right, where the dead girl lies on her bed. The Latin inscriptions beneath echo the gospel words, praising the woman's faith and recording Christ's command to the girl to rise. Painted on the south wall of St. Georg, the scene belongs to the cycle's culminating sequence of raisings from the dead.
facts: German Wikipedia counts this as the seventh scene of the cycle, the Raising of Jairus's Daughter, one of two scenes in which Christ appears twice.
It has been suggested that the north-wall miracles were chosen for their connection with water (the lake side), and the south-wall raisings from the dead for the side facing the presumed cemetery.
A slender tower at the left edge reappears, slightly shortened, in the Stilling of the Storm scene, linking the paintings visually.
wga:zearly/2/2paintin/5oberze5.notes: WGA titles this only by the first episode; the panel also shows the raising of Jairus's daughter (inscription includes 'surge puella'). Christ appears twice, as German Wikipedia notes for this scene. Dating disputed as for the rest of the cycle.
